Fly Lab · the maze guide

A fly-brain helicopter that finds its way

Can a tiny fly-like brain that has flown a route once or twice find its way back to it, from anywhere, using only a camera that points at the ground?

This is the second guide in the Fly Lab series. The first one teaches a simulated fly to tell faces apart. Here the same kind of brain leaves the lab and hovers over a hedge maze in the countryside, like the Queen's garden in Alice in Wonderland. It is shown a route through the maze. Then it is dropped somewhere else, facing any way, with no map and no line on the ground, and has to find the route and follow it to the exit.

14 × 20 camera pixels10–20 thousand memory cellsa route = 2.5 KBno map, no GPSdropped anywhere: 99% over six mazes
The short version Like an ant, the fly does not remember "turn left here". It remembers what the ground looked like along the route and steers toward whichever direction looks most familiar. That alone gets lost in look-alike hedge corridors: released near the route it reached the goal 13% of the time. Keeping a running guess of where it is on the route lifted that to 70%. Learning flights, and a memory of what every spot on the map looks like, let it be dropped anywhere and still reach the goal. A contrast filter keeps it working in fog and dusk, and averaging camera frames keeps it working at night. One trap: flying the route more than once fills the memory and made it lose in half of six mazes; flown once, it got within reach of the goal 99% of the time over all six (lab, 20,000 cells). It is all a simulation, and a small version of the fly runs right here in your browser.

How to read this guide

5 minutesJust the storyRead the short version above, then the "Where this leaves us" box at the end of each chapter. 20 minutesPlay alongEach chapter has a widget with a small fly you can run. Guess first where a "Predict first" box asks you to, then check. DeeperReproduce the numbersEvery table comes from runs of one command-line tool. Chapter 17 shows how to repeat them.

What the colours on the maps mean

The fly and its patch

the helicopter, pointing where it flies. The box around it is the ground its camera sees. With a swarm there is one coloured box per member.

What it has learned

green squares: ground along the route that it filed as "familiar". teal squares and lines: where its learning flights went.

Its flights

blue: following the route. orange line: heading for the route. A dashed green ring is where it believes it is on the map. A dot at the end: green = reached the goal, red = did not.

The world

start, goal. A white dashed line is the route it was shown (the fly never sees it). A red glow is "how alike does this place look".

Chapter 1

The world it flies over

What does the fly have to find its way through, and why is it built the way it is?

The maze stands in the countryside. Its hedges (tall and low, some with roses, some old stone walls, a few topiary balls) bend a little and vary in thickness and height. They stand on a lawn mowed in stripes, inside a gravel path. Around it are fields of different kinds (meadow, wheat, ploughed soil, rows of crops, orchards) with hedgerows between them, roads with centre lines, houses and barns, groves of trees and sometimes a pond. Everything has a height and a shadow from a low sun. The whole world is made by code, so any maze number gives a new one.

The first version of this world was a patchwork of pink checkers and blue ponds. It was much easier: every spot had its own colourful fingerprint. Inside a real hedge maze every corridor looks nearly the same, and that turns out to be the hard part.

The garden from above

the world the lab flies over
startgoalthe route (the fly never sees it)

A "changed version" has the same layout and route, but the flowers are elsewhere, the hedges bend a little differently and the light is a bit different. The fly is tested on it to see whether it recognises the place or only memorised a picture. Flip between the two and look for what changed.

The ideaA hedge maze is the hardest case for a fly that recognises places by how they look: every corridor looks like every other.

Why look-alike corridors are the hard part

Later, the fly will recognise where it is by its "fingerprint": the pattern of memory cells that fire for what its camera sees. So the first question is how alike different places look. Tap the map: the fly will compare the view at your tap with the view at every other place, and show where the look-alikes are.

  2. Tap the open lawn, then a field. Places with something distinctive (a pond, a house, a road) have few look-alikes, corridors have many.

Chapter 2

Camera, brain, and one look

How much of the world does the fly's camera get, and what does its brain make of a single look?

The helicopter is ideal: it always knows its compass heading, its speed and its height, and its camera always points straight down. The camera is the same eye as in the first guide, 14 rows × 20 columns = 280 sensors, lying on the ground below and turning with the fly. At the normal height it covers about 1.6 × 2.3 maze cells. Each sensor reports brightness and two colour differences (red–green and blue–yellow), and that is all the brain ever gets: 840 numbers per look.

Fly the camera around

drag on the map · turn · go higher or lower

The ground under the camera

What the fly gets: 20 × 14 sensors

Lower down, the camera sees a smaller, sharper patch. Higher up it sees more, blurrier. Try to find a spot where you can tell, from the 20 × 14 picture alone, where you are. That is the fly's job.

The ideaThe fly never stores a picture. It stores which of its memory cells fired, a short fingerprint, and later asks how many of today's cells it has met before.

The brain behind the camera, stage by stage

It is the same kind of brain as in the first guide, cut down to what this job needs: a memory centre and nothing else. Walk through it one stage at a time.

The fly's route memory is taught in the background the first time you tap. Green cells are ones that fired while it learned the route ("familiar"); red cells are new to it.

–Where this leaves us
The fly gets 840 numbers per look, turns them into a fingerprint of about 100 cells, and can ask how many of them it has met before. On the route roughly 35–40% are new, elsewhere 43–52%: a faint difference. Everything that follows is about getting a reliable steer out of it.
Chapter 3

Learning a route, the way an ant does

How can a fly follow a route without ever being told "turn left here"?

Ants and bees can retrace a route they walked a few times, and the leading idea is not that they memorise turns. They remember what the world looked like along the way, and at every step turn toward whichever direction looks most familiar. The fly's memory centre does exactly that:

  1. Fly the route once (with a teacher steering). Every view makes the Kenyon cells it uses "familiar". That is the whole memory. Nothing about the route is stored as a path. (Once is deliberate: every extra pass fills the memory, and a full memory says "familiar" about everything. Chapter 9 measures it.)
  2. To navigate, look in 9 directions (60° left to 60° right). For each, count how many of the firing cells are still unfamiliar. Fly the direction with the fewest.
The ideaFamiliar means "I have seen this before, from the route." The fly rolls downhill toward whatever looks most familiar.

Watch it learn

Before anything is flown, here is what teaching looks like. The fly (white, with its camera boxes around it) flies the route once with a teacher. Every square of ground it passes turns green: those are the views it filed under "familiar". Then it makes its learning flights: from spots all over the map it flies toward the route, and every square it crosses turns teal. Those squares are where it can later say "I have been here, and from here the route is that way". Pick a swarm first if you like: each coloured box is one member looking at its own patch of ground.

Chapter 4

Keeping track instead of guessing afresh

What if the fly did not decide from scratch at every step?

A single view is ambiguous in a look-alike corridor. A sequence of views, together with how far the fly has flown, is not. The ideal helicopter knows its heading and speed exactly (insects get the same from path integration), so it can keep a running guess of how far along the route it is:

  1. While learning the route, it also stores the pattern of firing cells at points along it, in order.
  2. While flying, it keeps a belief over "where on the route am I?". Each step the belief is moved on by its own flying, blurred a little for uncertainty, and sharpened by how well the current view matches the views stored there.
  3. It then prefers directions that match the route's direction at its best guess, as firmly as it is sure, and lets the familiarity scan correct sideways drift.
The ideaA look-alike corridor fools one look, but not a whole sequence of looks plus the distance flown.

"Keeping track", step by step

How it keeps track along the route

tap a step

Go back to the widget in chapter 3, switch the steering to "+ keep track" and repeat "Try 8 releases near the route". In the lab this took a single fly from 13% to 70% (and from 47% to 91% of the route flown). A short gap where the route is out of sight (up to 1.5 cells) is bridged by its own motion; only a longer loss resets the belief. After a single flight with tracking on, the chart under the map shows the belief following the fly.

Try this
  1. In chapter 3, switch to "+ keep track" and press "Fly it" from a spot near the route. Look at the chart: the red dots hug the line.
  2. Now compare 8 releases with and without tracking. The in-page fly is smaller than the lab's (10,000 cells, a small map, 8 releases): expect the same direction, not the same figures.
70%Where this leaves us
A fly that remembers where it has been follows the route through look-alike corridors. But we only ever released it next to the route. Next: drop it anywhere.
Chapter 5

Dropped anywhere

How can the fly find the route from a place it has never been near?

Ants do not only learn the route. Around their nest they make learning walks, looking back at the nest from many spots, which lets them find their way home from nearly anywhere close. The maze fly copies that:

  1. Learning flights. After learning the route, the fly flies from spots all over the map toward the route and keeps those views in a second memory (the mushroom body keeps different memories in different compartments). This one is graded: each view halves the "novelty" of the cells it uses.
  2. Two-stage navigation. Until the route itself looks familiar, follow the second memory; then switch to the route memory.
  3. Know where you are on the map. During the learning flights the fly also stores, for every spot, the view turned to face north (its compass lets it turn its camera image, so one stored view per spot fits whatever way it faces). Dropped somewhere, it keeps a belief over the whole map, moved by its own flying and sharpened by matching, and once sure flies straight for the route.
The ideaMake a map out of views, not lines: know where you are from what you see, then head for the route.

"Knowing where it is on the map", in plain words

This phrase hides a lot, so here it is slowly. It does not mean the fly has a drawing of the maze, coordinates, or GPS. It means the fly owns a big lookup table: for thousands of spots on the ground, "at this spot, looking north, the camera fingerprint was this". Dropped somewhere, it asks: which spot in my table looks most like what I see now? That spot is its guess. One look is sometimes fooled, so it keeps a set of guesses that it updates as it flies. Walk through it:

How it knows where it is

tap a step
What is stored

About 2,000 to 3,000 north-up fingerprints, each tagged with the spot it was taken at, and nothing else. Roughly 100 cell numbers per fingerprint, so a few hundred thousand numbers in all: well under a megabyte.

What "north-up" means

The camera turns with the helicopter, so the same place looks different facing east or west. The fly's compass lets it rotate its picture so north is always at the top. Then one stored fingerprint per spot fits whichever way it is facing.

What "belief" means

Not one guess but a score for every spot, added up like votes. Flying moves all the scores along by the distance flown, blurring them a little, and every new look boosts the spots that match. After a few steps one spot stands out. How far the votes are spread tells the fly how sure it is.

What it is used for

Only to head for the route. Once the guess is confident, the fly aims at the nearest point of the route it remembers (from its own odometry while it learned it), and follows that as firmly as it is sure. When it reaches the route, the route memory takes over.

What it cannot do

Places that look alike (a corridor, a field of ploughed soil) get similar scores, so it can be fooled there. It only knows places its learning flights visited, and it forgets nothing but also learns nothing new while flying.

Why it is the big one

Route memory says "this looks like the route", which is a faint clue (chapter 2). The map gives a second, independent clue, "I am about here", which is what turns a lost fly into one that flies straight for the route.

Why the second memory is graded

The route memory is a yes-or-no flag. The learning flights show the fly thousands of views, and a yes-or-no memory fills up. Drag the slider to store more views and watch both kinds of memory fill (the views are north-up views from the learning flights).

Yes-or-no versus graded memory

drag to store more views

Yes-or-no: has this cell ever fired?

Graded: how often has it fired? (brighter = more)

Drag the slider. The first move teaches the fly in the background (a few seconds).

The landscape, with the second memory

Back in chapter 3 the "Rolling downhill" widget has a second button. Choose "Approach memory": the yellow is now a wide, faint funnel around the route, and the arrows lean toward it. The widget counts how many do. That small lean is what the learning flights bought, and it is the reason chapter 5 also needs the map belief.

Where am I on the map?

Where am I on the map?

one look, then a guess

Tap the map to put the fly down. Its compass turns what the camera sees so north is up, so which way it faces does not matter. It compares that view with the view stored at every spot; the red glow shows how well each place matches, and the green ring is its best guess.

Weather
Tap the map. (The first time, it learns the map: a few seconds.)

A single look is usually enough but not always: for this small in-page fly, across 40 random spots in clear weather, the best guess was within 0.6 of a maze cell 75% of the time (median error 0.3 cell), and a look-alike place fooled it the rest. In fog without the filter it was never right (0%); with the filter, 65%. The real flight does not rely on one look: the fly keeps a belief that its own motion carries forward and each new look sharpens, and in the lab its guess was then typically off by only 0.15 cell. Turning the views north-up matters: without it the lab's fly was off by almost 7 cells, because views taken facing other ways rarely match.

The lab's numbers: 2 mazes × 2 flies × 10 drops, normal height, each good to about ±8 points. Learning flights raised the share that found the route from 45% to 77% but not the share that reached the goal: finding the route is not the same as staying on it.

Watch out The ladder was measured on mazes 1 and 2 with the route flown three times. Chapter 9 tries six mazes and finds this number is not general: with three passes the average was 54%. The cause is the route memory filling up, and flying the route once fixes it.
100%Where this leaves us
With learning flights, tracking and a map, every fly in the lab test found its way from a random drop to the goal at normal height. What if it is flying low, or the weather turns? Next.
Chapter 6

High and low

What happens when the helicopter is lower or higher than when it learned?

A helicopter cannot always fly at the same height. Height changes what the camera sees: lower, a smaller and sharper patch; higher, a larger and blurrier one. Use the height slider in the camera widget in chapter 2 to see it. For the fly it is the same problem as viewing distance was for faces, and the lab's numbers show it clearly: a fly that learned at one height and is flown low does worse than a fly flying blind. Every view looks unfamiliar and the answers all tip the same way.

The ideaA memory is only good at the height it was made. Practise at several heights, and keep one memory for each.

Press the button to measure it in the page. For three flies, the widget measures how much newer a random spot away from the route looks than a spot on the route, at heights from 0.5 to 1.5. A bigger gap means a clearer signal for steering.

The height cliff

Reached the goal / share of the route flown, released near the route (measured in the first, colourful world). A blind straight flight flies 53% of these routes.

  • Practise at several heights. The cliff nearly disappears.
  • Keep a memory per height. The helicopter knows its height, so it can use the memory made at the closest height. This helps most when low, and stops one memory filling up.
  • Use a small swarm (chapter 8): about +7 points on top.

With everything switched on, the fly reached the goal from a random drop 95% of the time at normal height and 93% flown low.

93%Where this leaves us
Height is manageable if the fly has practised at several heights and knows its altitude. Weather is next.
Chapter 7

Fog, dusk and night

What if the day is not the day it learned the route?

The same landscape looks different in different weather. Haze and fog fade everything toward grey, dusk is dark and orange, night is dark and grainy, and a cheap camera adds speckle. A fly that learned the route in clear weather sees a route full of unfamiliar views and gets lost. The cure is a contrast filter: stretch every view so its brightness always has the same spread, like the gain control in real eyes.

The ideaStretch every view to the same contrast and fog stops mattering. Average several frames and night stops mattering too (chapter 9).

Chapter 8

Many flies, one camera

How do the swarm tricks from the face guide carry over?

The first guide found that a swarm only helps if its members see differently. Here the swarm is a set of "virtual flies" sharing one camera frame and one wiring: each member looks at its own patch of ground (its own centre of gaze), and every member's opinion about the nine directions is added up. Each extra member costs only its own set of familiar-or-not flags. A drone camera has far more pixels than a fly's eye, so a wide, sharp frame can be divided among members.

The ideaSeveral looks at slightly different patches of ground are worth more than one look repeated, as long as the members see different things.

Chapter 9

Breaking it on purpose

How much can the world go wrong before the fly fails?

The results so far were for an ideal helicopter. A real drone is pushed by wind, and its idea of where it is (from its own motion) drifts. Meanwhile night was the one weather the contrast filter could not fix. We ran experiments on both. Each one changes one thing and measures the same "got within 0.8 cells of the goal" as before.

The ideaBreak one thing at a time and measure. Some of what looks fragile is not, and some of what looks solid (the maze itself) is.

Wind and a bad odometer

Two different problems. Wind pushes the helicopter sideways without the fly knowing: what it sees is still true. A bad odometer makes the fly's belief wrong: the belief on the route and on the map is moved on by its own motion, so a wrong estimate of heading or distance moves it to the wrong place.

Try to break it

the full fly (learning flights + tracking + map)
Swarm
Set the wind and the odometer errors, then drop the fly.

The chart: the line is where the fly really is along the route; the red dots where it thinks it is. A bad odometer pulls them apart.

These three tables used mazes 1 and 2 with three route passes. Unknown wind costs the most, but not much: 90% for the ideal helicopter, 88% with a wind of a fifth of the flying speed, 80% at two fifths. The odometer errors cost even less: a constant 17° heading error still got 80%, a jittery compass 93%, a distance reading 25% too long 90%. Most of these are inside the ±8-point noise of the ideal figure. The reason is that the belief is only a starting guess: at every step the stored views pull it back to where the fly really is, and the steering itself follows what it sees.

Night

At night the picture is dark and grainy, and the contrast filter stretches the noise with the signal (chapter 7: 28%). A real camera can take many frames while the fly moves one step and average them, which cuts the noise by the square root of the number of frames. Another cheap option is to smooth each view over its neighbours. Both change what the brain gets, so the fly must also learn the route with the same processing.

Everything at once (stress test)

A last stress test: night, with the filter and 16 frames per step, and a wind of 30% of the flying speed, and an odometer that is 0.2 rad (11°) off with noise of 0.1 rad each step. Result: 93% got within 0.8 cells of the goal (2 mazes × 2 flies × 10 drops). Each problem on its own was survivable; so, it turns out, is the pile of them.

These used mazes 1 and 2 with three route passes; over six mazes with one pass and 16 frames the night result held (see the last table of this chapter). Night with the contrast filter alone got 20% in this run (28% in chapter 7's run; the difference is chance). Averaging 4 camera frames per step gave 80%, and 16 frames 93%, as good as clear weather. The filter is still needed: 16 frames without it got 8%. Smoothing every view needs no extra frames and got 77%, or 85% together with 4 frames. In a moonless night, with a tenth of the light, 16 frames lifted 13% to 48% and 64 frames to 77%, so it is noise-limited: more frames keep helping. A foggy night got 40%. To picture 16 frames: a camera at 30 frames per second on a drone flying 10 m/s at 50 m height has about 18 frames in the 0.6 s it takes to fly one step.

The maze itself

Everything above used the same maze, or the two mazes the fly was developed on. That flatters it. Making four more mazes (the same generator, different seeds) showed something else: in some mazes the fly is nearly perfect and in others it is lost almost every time. Across six 6 × 6 mazes, with 16 drops each, the full fly (route flown three times) got within 0.8 cells of the goal 81%, 94%, 88%, 0%, 25% and 25% of the time: 54% overall, not the 95–100% of the first two.

The same fly, different mazes

each maze teaches its own fly (about 10 seconds)
Pick a maze and press "Try 8 drops". The first time each maze takes about 10 seconds to teach.

The six mazes of the lab test (numbers in the dots). Rings: the route flown three times; filled dots: flown once. With three passes longer routes tended to do worse, but not always: maze 6 is not longer than maze 3 and still failed. With one pass all six are near 100%.

Why: the route memory fills up

Chapter 2 showed that one look is only a faint clue: the share of new cells is a few points lower on the route than off it. The fly decides "I am on the route" when the best of its nine directions looks at least as familiar as a fixed level (12% of the firing cells new). That level suits a memory that is about half full. But the yes-or-no route memory fills as the route gets longer and the fly flies it more often. In a maze with a long route it fills to 80%, almost every view then looks familiar everywhere, and the fly believes it is on the route while it is far from it. It never uses its map, and wanders off. In a short-route maze the opposite can happen: the level is never reached.

MazeRoute (cells)Memory full after 3 passesNew cells on the routeNew cells elsewhereLab: near the goal (3 passes)Lab: near the goal (1 pass)
112.160%16%20%81%94%
29.852%25%30%94%100%
315.962%13%21%88%100%
421.779%4%8%0%100%
524.477%5%9%25%100%
614.971%10%10%25%100%

Memory fullness and the two "new cells" columns: measured on the in-page fly (10,000 cells, best of 9 directions, 30–40 places each). The lab columns: the full fly, 2 flies × 8 drops per maze.

Look at maze 6: on the route and off it look equally new (10% and 10%), so no level can tell them apart from one view. Mazes 4 and 5 have a route memory so full that everything is below 12%.

The fix: learn the route once

If the memory is what fills up, put less into it. Flying the route once instead of three times, with the same 20,000 memory cells, took the six-maze average from 54% to 99% of drops that got near the goal. Two passes gave 75%: the more times the route is flown, the worse. It is a case where more practice hurts, because a memory that says "familiar" about everything says nothing.

The second fix: let the fly measure its own "on the route" level

The fixed level of 12% is the deeper flaw: whatever the memory looks like, the fly should not need a number somebody chose. So after learning, the fly now measures it. It looks at views a little off the route (facing roughly along it) and at views far from it, notes how new the best of its nine directions looks in each case, and puts its "on the route" level a quarter of the way from the first to the second. With three passes this took the six mazes from 54% to 83% (halfway between the two: 76%).

Alone, flying the route once helps in small mazes (99% in six 6 × 6 mazes) but stops working as the route gets longer: 67% at 8 × 8, 38% at 10 × 10 and 8% at 12 × 12. Together the two fixes gave 94%, 92%, 90% and 92% at those sizes (chapter 14). Both are now the maze app's defaults.

Watch out The first numbers in this guide (and the "95–100%" in the short version) were measured on mazes 1 and 2 with three route passes. Those two happen to have a memory that is neither empty nor full. Measured over six mazes, the answer was 54%, until the route was flown once.

Then, in bad conditions, over six mazes

night, filter and 16 frames per step92%
wind of 40% of the flying speed79%
odometer heading off by 17°97%

6 mazes × 2 flies × 6 drops each, about ±7 points. The wind, odometer and night tables above used mazes 1 and 2 with three route passes.

Try this
  1. Set a wind of 40% and press "Try 8 drops". Then set the odometer heading error to 17° and repeat. Compare with the table.
  2. In chapter 5's widget, switch to night, turn on the filter, then the frames setting to 16, and drop it a few times.
–Where this leaves us
Wind, a bad odometer and night barely hurt the fly, and night is fixed by averaging frames. What did hurt was the maze itself: a route memory that fills up. Fixing that (fly the route once, and let the fly measure its own “on the route” level) took six mazes from 54% to 94–99%, and made 12 × 12 mazes work.
Chapter 10

Roll, pitch and yaw

What if the helicopter is not level, and not sure which way north is?

So far the camera looked straight down from a helicopter that flew perfectly level. A real one is never level. It rolls (one side dips), pitches (nose up or down) and yaws (turns around its vertical axis: that is its heading). The camera is bolted to the body, so when the body tilts, the camera looks at a different patch of ground, and because the lens is wide, the patch is also stretched on the side that is leaning away. Yaw does two other things: the compass reading is what turns the camera picture "north-up" for the map (chapter 5), and the heading is what the odometer adds up when it keeps track (chapter 4).

Tilt the helicopter

the white box is where a level camera looks, the red one where the tilted camera looks

Tilted camera

Level camera (what it learned)

Try this
  1. Roll 15°, pitch 0: the red box slides sideways by a fifth of its length and the right side stretches (perspective).
  2. Turn on compensation with an error of 3°: the boxes nearly coincide again.
  3. Push the pitch to 40°: the camera looks half a box backwards, and the picture it gets has little in common with the learned one.
The ideaA tilt or a wrong heading does not make the fly blind. It makes the picture shift and the map rotate, and the fly can be given sensors that undo most of it.

How a real fly copes

A fly does not wait to be told it has tilted. The halteres, two tiny club-shaped hind wings, act as gyroscopes and report rotation; the fly's neck turns the head against the body's roll, so the eyes keep looking at the same piece of the world. The three ocelli on top of the head sense where the sky is brighter than the ground, which is a horizon sensor. A strip of the eye's upper edge senses the polarised light of the sky, a compass that does not drift. Each of these maps onto something a drone has (a gyroscope, a horizon estimate, a sky or magnetic compass), and all of them can be fed into the fly's brain as "sensor" inputs. Chapter 11 lists them all.

What we tested

The test helicopter's roll and pitch wander randomly and slowly (the tilt from one step to the next is 80% the same, like a gust), with the standard deviation in the table. The fly learned the route in calm air. "Compensated" means it counter-rotates its camera by its own attitude estimate, so only the error of the estimate is left. Six mazes × 2 flies × 6 drops each, dropped anywhere, one route pass and the calibrated level (94% with no tilt), about ±7 points.

Roll and pitch (standard deviation)Got within 0.8 cells of the goal
5°93%
10°86%
20°90%
35°78%
45°56%
20°, compensated exactly93%
20°, compensated with a 3° error90%
20°, compensated with a 6° error (an ocelli-like horizon sensor)94%
35°, compensated with a 3° error90%
10°, and the route also practised in rough air79%
20°, and the route also practised in rough air79%
Yaw: the compass is wrongGot within 0.8 cells of the goal
a compass that is off by about 6° (0.1 rad) every step, without accumulating (a sky compass)86%
17° (0.3 rad)87%
34° (0.6 rad)79%
57° (1.0 rad)74%
a gyro compass whose error random-walks by 0.01 rad per step (about 0.2 rad after a 400-step flight)94%
0.03 rad per step89%
0.08 rad per step89%
0.15 rad per step75%

Tilts up to 20° cost nothing we could measure (the reference is 94%, and differences under about 7 points are noise). At 35° the fly drops to 78% and at 45° to 56%; counter-rotating the camera with a 3° estimate error brings 35° back to 90%. So attitude sensing matters only for big tilts, but then it pays well. Practising the route in rough air made it worse (79%, 79%): the memory then holds shifted, stretched views of every place, which makes everything look familiar. A compass that is off by 6–17° at every step cost little; at 34° to 57° it cost 15 to 20 points. A gyro compass that drifts by 0.01 to 0.08 rad per step was harmless, and only 0.15 rad per step (several radians over a flight, so north is lost) hurt clearly. Why so robust: steering compares nine looks taken from the same tilted camera, so a tilt shifts all of them alike, and the map belief gathers many looks, so a single wrong one is outvoted.

Try this
  1. In chapter 9's "Try to break it" widget, which now has sliders for roll and pitch, the compass and an optic-flow odometer, set the roll and pitch to 20° and press "Try 8 drops". Then switch on "Counter-rotate the camera".
  2. Set the compass error to 0.5 rad and watch the dashed green ring: the map guess gets worse before the fly does.
–Where this leaves us
Roll, pitch and yaw errors that would worry a pilot barely worry this fly until they get large: tilts over 30° and compass errors of half a radian or more. A gyro to steady the camera and a compass that does not drift buy back most of what is lost.
Chapter 11

All of the fly's senses

A fly is more than an eye. Which of its other senses could help a helicopter find its way?

Until now the maze fly had one sense: a downward camera. A real fly has a whole sensor suite, and each of its parts has a counterpart on a drone. Tap a sense to see what it does, what the drone's version is, what it could give the navigator, and whether we tested it.

The fly's senses and a drone's

tap a sense
Fly senseA drone's versionWhat it adds for navigationTested here
Compound eyesThe cameraViews of the ground: everything so faryes
Motion vision (optic flow)Optic-flow sensorGround speed and drift, including the windyes: wind 40% 69% → 78%, wind 70% 33% → 44%
HalteresGyroscope (an IMU)Roll and pitch for counter-rotating the camera; heading changeyes: chapter 10
OcelliA horizon or sky-brightness sensorA coarse attitude without gyros (5–10° error); light level for exposureyes, as a 6° attitude error
Polarised-light compassSky polarisation or magnetic compassAn absolute heading that does not driftyes: compass error without and with accumulation, chapter 10
Antennae (Johnston's organ)Airspeed and vibration sensorSpeed through the air, not over the ground: alone it cannot see the windimplied by the odometer without optic flow
Antennae (smell)Chemical sensorsLandmarks by odour, plume followingno
Bristles and strain sensorsContact and whisker sensorsBumping into a hedge, a last resortno
Temperature and humidityWeather sensorsLittle for this jobno

Putting several together

Roll, pitch, wind and compass errors all at once (tilt 10°, compass 6° each step, wind of 40% of the flying speed) got within 0.8 cells of the goal 69% of the time. With the camera counter-rotated to within 3°, a better compass (3° each step) and an optic-flow odometer, 78%. A harsher pile (tilt 35°, compass 34°, wind 70%) got 14%, and with the sensors above, 44%.

Keep in mind Every sense here is a correction to something the camera-only fly already does. None of them replaces the camera. The camera fingerprints say where the fly is; the other senses say how it moved and how it is leaning, so the fly can trust the fingerprints more.
–Where this leaves us
No extra sense was needed for the mazes in this guide: the camera does the navigating. The other senses are insurance. Optic flow helps in strong wind, a gyro in big tilts, a steady compass in big heading errors, and together they turned the harshest test (tilt 35°, compass error 34°, wind of 70% of the flying speed) from 14% to 44%.
Chapter 12

Bigger swarms, and other ways to go further

What does a bigger swarm buy, and which other tricks make a fly see more?

A swarm is several virtual flies that share one camera and one wiring, each looking at its own patch of ground (chapter 8). Every member adds its opinion about the nine directions. This chapter asks what a bigger or cleverer swarm adds, for the maze fly and for the fly in the main Fly Lab app that tells men from women.

A circle of gaze

Each member looks a little ahead, behind, left or right of the centre. The simplest way to make members see different things. Used in chapters 3–9.

Three circles in a row

Seven members in three small rings across the frame: the widest spread of patches (chapter 8).

Different zoom levels

One member looks at the ground at normal size, one close up, one wide. A close view has detail, a wide view has context, and all three change together when the height changes.

A swarm that votes on the map

The members' north-up fingerprints are added up when the fly works out where it is. Available in the lab tool (--map-swarm); with the maze results this good we had little room to show a gain.

Boosting

The swarm joins in rounds. After each round the photos (or places) it still gets wrong are shown more often to the next round, so newcomers become specialists. Used for the face fly.

Different viewing distances

In the face fly, members can also look from slightly nearer or further. One more way to differ (tested below).

In the maze: height is where a swarm pays

In clear weather at the height it learned at, a swarm added little to the maze fly (chapter 8: +7 points, before the fixes of chapter 9). The zoomed swarm was really meant for another problem: flying at a height the fly did not practise. Learned at height 1 and flown low (0.6) or high (1.5), six mazes, dropped anywhere, one route pass:

Flown at heightOne flySwarm of 3 (circle)Swarm of 3 at different zooms
0.6 (low)60%64%69%
1.5 (high)71%–69%

6 mazes × 2 flies × 6 drops, about ±7 points. The fly learned at height 1 only, in one memory.

Flown low (0.6) one fly got 60%, a circle of three 64%, and three members at different zoom levels 69%. The zoom levels move together when the height changes, so one member always sees something close to what was learned. Flown high (1.5) the single fly already did well (71%) and the zoomed swarm did not add (69%): a higher, wider view only blurs detail, which costs little. So a zoomed swarm buys robustness mostly when flying lower than learned.

For faces: a swarm of 25 that boosts

The face fly of the main app is a different job (men or women, from 32 × 32 photos) but the same idea. One fly scores about 60% on 500 photos it never saw. With 25 flies, each looking from its own point of a circle and trained in rounds, the swarm reached 68–69%. The swarm is now built into the app: Train tab, step 3b.

Faces: one fly and swarms

share of 500 new photos right (men and women counted equally)
One fly
60%
A swarm of 9 (circle of gaze)
65%
25 flies that boost, equal votes
68.1%
…votes weighted by each fly's say, 300 sessions each
69.2%

68.5%

One run each, about ±2 points. More flies and longer practice stop adding past 25 flies and 300 sessions; boosting only pays off from about 15 flies (a boosting swarm of 10 scored 61% against 64% without). Looking from different distances as well (0.9, 1 and 1.1 of the set distance, or 0.85 to 1.15) made no difference (68.8% and 66.7% with equal votes, 68.2% and 69.0% weighted), and the circle of gaze has a sweet spot near 10° (6°: 66.7%, 15°: 65.1%).

Keep in mind A swarm is worth having only when its members make different mistakes. Flies that look at the same thing vote alike and gain about a point. Flies that look at different patches, distances or zoom levels, or that specialise on what the others get wrong, gain 5 to 9 points. That is the same lesson for faces and for mazes.
–Where this leaves us
A swarm is worth having when its members differ: in the maze, different zoom levels when flying low (+9 points); for faces, 25 flies that each look from their own spot and train on what the others get wrong (60% → 68–69%, now in the app). Past 25 flies, or with longer practice, nothing more was gained.

Chapter 14

How big a maze, and how long would it take?

Could this fly a real area, like 100 × 100 maze cells, or 1,000 × 1,000?

Training time is dominated by the learning flights, because they cover the whole map, so it grows with the area. Learning the route itself grows only with its length. Move the sliders to plan a real flight: one maze cell is taken to be about the flying height, since the camera sees a patch of ground roughly 1.5 times as long as it is high.

Bigger maps need four changes: build the landscape in tiles around the helicopter; search only near the believed position; keep a separate memory for each region (the route memory already fills half its cells by 6 × 6); and learn in a corridor around the route instead of the whole map. 1,000 × 1,000 is not possible as built.
95%Where this leaves us
The recipe scales to about a kilometre in principle, at hours of computing and a few hours of real flying with a survey. Beyond that, the memory needs splitting.
Chapter 15

Where else the same trick could work

Who would want a tiny brain that repeats a route it was shown once?

"Visual teach and repeat" is a real technique in robotics: show a robot a route once, and it repeats it using a camera. What is unusual here is how small it is: one yes-or-no flag per memory cell, 2.5 KB per route, no map, no GPS, and a brain that could run on a camera board costing a few dollars. Some ideas, none tried outside the simulation:

JobWhat is taughtWhat could go wrong
Drone inspection where GPS is weakA pilot flies the route once (a barn, a greenhouse, under a bridge, along a warehouse aisle); the drone repeats itChanging light, moved goods, wind
Safe return homeThe outward flight becomes the route; if GPS is lost or jammed, retrace itThe way back looks different from the way out (turn the camera, or learn both)
Farm rows and orchardsOne pass along the rows; repeat each weekCrops grow and change colour: the memory ages
Robot lawnmowers and delivery robotsWalk the route once with a remoteMoving people and cars; a camera looking forward, not down
Pipes, tunnels and underwaterA route through look-alike surroundings, where keeping track (chapter 4) matters mostVery little to see; murky water is "fog" (chapter 7)
Many cheap cameras votingThe swarm from chapter 8, one camera or severalEach camera must be trained where it stands

The same brain, other jobs

Telling things apart

The face guide's fly learns from yes/no feedback on a device with no network: sorting ripe from unripe fruit, flagging defects on a line with an operator's button as the reward, camera traps sorting "animal / no animal".

Many looks, one decision

Several cheap cameras looking at slightly different parts of one object and voting: a bigger gain than the same view repeated, as the face guide found.

Anything with a sparse memory

Any job that can be phrased as "have I seen something like this before?" fits the yes-or-no memory: place recognition, anomaly spotting, "is this the usual scene?"

95%Where this leaves us
The promise is a route memory of a few kilobytes on a tiny camera board. The catch is everything a simulation leaves out. Next: exactly what that is.
Chapter 16

What this does not show

How far can the results be trusted?

  • It is a simulation. The world is generated by code, not photographed. The pictures are drawn, not real, and nothing here has flown a real drone.
  • An almost ideal helicopter. It knows its heading, speed and height, and the camera always points straight down. Chapter 9 gave it wind and a bad odometer, but not a wobbling, tilting camera or a changing height between frames.
  • A still world. No cars or people move, the sun never moves, nothing grows. Weather is simulated as changes to the picture (fade, darken, tint, speckle), not photographed.
  • Small samples. Each figure comes from 20–40 drops, good to about ±8 points, on a few mazes of one kind.
  • Small mazes. The lab's results are mostly on 6 × 6 mazes, with a few on 10 × 10. Bigger mazes hit memory and compute limits (chapter 14).
  • The in-page fly is smaller. The widgets use 10,000 cells and a small map so they run in a browser tab; their numbers differ from the lab's, and 8 releases is a tiny sample.
  • Hardware estimates are estimates. The camera-board sizes and times come from counting operations, not from a board.
95%Where this leaves us
Good enough to be worth a real test, far from proof. Try it yourself next.
Chapter 17

Try it, run it

How do I fly it myself?

Open the Maze app Build a maze (size, wobble, variety), teach the fly the route at chosen heights, tap anywhere on the map to drop it, and watch what it sees and how unfamiliar each direction looks. Change its height mid-flight, switch on the swarm layouts, the wrong-way memory or climbing, pick the weather and the contrast filter, and fly over a changed version of the maze.

To reproduce the lab's numbers, the command-line tool tools/route.mjs in the flyfy repository runs the same experiments. For example, the full setup, dropped anywhere, in fog with the filter:

node tools/route.mjs --cells 6 --setups colour --policy familiar --kc 20000 --sparsity 0.01 \
  --drop --approach 1 --track --map --swarm 3 --normalize --weather fog

Chapter 19

Words to know

Familiarity navigation
Following a route by turning toward whichever direction looks most familiar, the way ants and bees are thought to do it.
Kenyon cells
The fly's learning centre. Each cell reads a few random inputs and only a few percent fire at once, so every view gets its own sparse code.
Route memory
One yes-or-no flag per Kenyon cell: has this cell been used while flying the route?
Approach memory
A second, graded memory made during the learning flights, used to find the route from anywhere.
Learning flights
Flights from many spots toward the route (or nest), used to learn what the way back looks like from everywhere.
Path integration (odometry)
Keeping track of where you are from your own movement: heading and distance flown.
Knowing where it is on the map
Having a lookup table of "spot → north-up fingerprint" made during the learning flights, and finding the spot that best matches what the camera sees now, sharpened over several steps by the distance flown. It is not a drawing or GPS.
Keeping track
Holding a score for every point along the route and moving it forward by the distance flown, then boosting the points whose stored fingerprint matches the current view.
Belief
A spread of guesses of where the fly is, each with a weight; it is moved by flying, blurred a little, and sharpened by what the camera sees.
North-up view
The camera image turned to face north with the compass, so views taken facing different ways can be compared.
Contrast filter
Stretching each view so its brightness always has the same spread, so fog and dim light stop changing what the fly sees.
Burst averaging
Taking several camera frames per step and averaging them: the noise shrinks by the square root of the number of frames.
Swarm
Several virtual flies sharing one camera and one wiring, each looking at its own patch; their opinions are added up.
Drop
Putting the fly down somewhere on the map, facing any direction, and letting it find its own way.
Maze cell
The unit of size here: one square of the maze, about the flying height when seen from a real drone.
Fly Lab · the maze guide. The garden, the route and the lab's figures come from this project's simulations and can be reproduced with the tools in web/tools/. The in-page fly is a smaller version that runs in your browser.
